## Why This Matters

L01 traced the air-quality question — *which town had the worst air last year?* — through the
five stages but never touched data. This lesson picks up the **toolkit**: the two libraries
you will use in every later unit, and the first real **Clean** step.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
**NumPy is the engine; pandas is the dashboard.** NumPy gives you raw numeric horsepower —
arrays of numbers you can compute on all at once. pandas wraps that in a labeled table with
named columns and rows you can actually read. You drive with the dashboard, but the engine is
doing the work underneath.
:::

## The Toolkit

Almost all data work in Python sits on a small, stable stack. The two foundations:

| Library | Gives you | You reach for it when |
|---------|-----------|------------------------|
| **NumPy** | the `ndarray`: a fast, fixed-type array; vectorized math | you have many numbers of one type and want speed |
| **pandas** | the `DataFrame`: a labeled table (columns + index), built on NumPy | you have a *table* with named, mixed-type columns |

pandas is built *on top of* NumPy, so they fit together: a DataFrame column is essentially a
NumPy array with a label.

## Core Ideas

### NumPy arrays

| Idea | What it means |
|------|---------------|
| **`ndarray`** | a grid of values, **all the same type**, of any dimension (1-D vector, 2-D matrix, ...) |
| **`shape`** | the size along each dimension, e.g. `(6,)` or `(2, 2)` |
| **`dtype`** | the single element type, e.g. `float64`, `int64` |
| **Vectorization** | one operation applied to the whole array at once (`arr.mean()`, `arr > 15`) — shorter and far faster than a Python loop |

### pandas DataFrame and Series

| Idea | What it means |
|------|---------------|
| **`DataFrame`** | a 2-D table: named columns, an index, **a different type allowed per column** |
| **`Series`** | one column of a DataFrame (a labeled 1-D array) |
| **Inspect** | `.head()`, `.info()` (columns, non-null counts, dtypes), `.describe()` (numeric summary) |
| **Select / filter** | `df["col"]` (a Series), `df[df["col"] > x]` (rows by condition) |

### Tidy (rectangular) data

::: {.callout-note}
**Tidy data:** one **row per observation**, one **column per variable**, and **one proper
type per column**. It is the shape every later tool — EDA, modeling, plotting — expects, so
getting there is the goal of the first clean.
:::

## When to Use NumPy vs. pandas

- **Use NumPy when:** the data is purely numeric and uniform — vectors, matrices, image
  pixels — and you want raw speed without labels.
- **Use pandas when:** you have a *table* with named columns of mixed types (text, dates,
  numbers, categories) — which is almost every real dataset.
- **Avoid:** hand-written Python loops over rows for arithmetic that a vectorized NumPy or
  pandas call would do in one line.

## A First Clean (preview)

The lab builds a small air-quality table with two realistic defects — missing readings and a
numeric column stored as text — and fixes both:

```python
# Illustrative (the runnable version is in the lab)
aq["pm25"] = aq["pm25"].fillna(aq["pm25"].median())          # fill gaps with the median
aq["temp_c"] = pd.to_numeric(aq["temp_c"].str.replace(",", ".", regex=False))  # text -> number
```

The payoff is a tidy table that `.describe()` will fully summarize — a text column is silently
skipped until its type is fixed.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Reading `.describe()` and forgetting the text columns.** Columns left as `object` are not
  summarized; check `.info()` for surprise `object` dtypes before trusting a summary.
- **Filling missing values without thinking.** The median is a safe default here, but the
  *right* choice depends on why the data is missing — a topic for the EDA unit.
- **Looping in Python for array math.** It is slower and longer than the vectorized call.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Why not just use Excel, or plain Python lists?"** — Excel is fine for a quick look but does
not scale, version, or reproduce: you cannot rerun it on a fresh file and trust identical
steps. Plain Python lists have no vectorized math and no labels. NumPy and pandas give you
**reproducible, fast, labeled** data work — the reason they are the field's default tools.

## Quiz Hooks

*The things to retain — these feed the L02 retrieval quiz at the start of L03.*

- A NumPy array has a **shape** and a single **dtype**; **vectorized** ops beat Python loops 
- A **DataFrame** is a labeled table with mixed-type columns; an **ndarray** is raw numbers of one type 
- **Detect and handle missing values** with `isnull().sum()` then `fillna(...)` 
- **Tidy data**: one row per observation, one column per variable, one type per column 
- A **text (object) column is not summarized** by `.describe()` until its type is fixed
